claims.claim_vi: Microprocessors commonly store the individual bytes of a value in memory in one of two byte orders, called byte ordering or endian nature.
claims.verified_by: Source body read from the pinned commit; the statement is in the source text.

claims.claim_vi: Intel x86 processors store a two-byte integer with the least significant byte first (little endian).
claims.verified_by: Source body read from the pinned commit; the statement is in the source text.

claims.claim_vi: In big endian the most significant byte is at the lowest memory address; older PowerPC and Motorola 68k often use big endian; network communications and file storage use big endian.
claims.verified_by: Source body read from the pinned commit; the statement is in the source text.

claims.claim_vi: Byte order matters when data moves between systems or is processed by systems with different endianness; it must be handled correctly.
claims.verified_by: Source body read from the pinned commit; the statement is in the source text.

claims.claim_vi: Python struct documentation: the number 1023 (0x3ff) is 03 ff in big endian and ff 03 in little endian; network order is big-endian; native order depends on the host; Intel x86, AMD64 and Apple M1 are little-endian, IBM z and many legacy architectures big-endian; sys.byteorder tells the host order.
claims.verified_by: Read from a raw copy at the pinned commit in the URL (a later change to the default branch does not alter it).

claims.claim_vi: Reading ff 03 as a big-endian unsigned two-byte integer gives 0xff03 = 65283 (computed by the author).
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against primary documentation.

claims.claim_vi: Byte order concerns the order of bytes of a number, not of bits within a byte.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against primary documentation.
